stem: An adult woman from Rawalpindi presents with chronic constipation for the past 6 months, with straining and a sensation of incomplete evacuation. Her diet is adequate in fibre and she drinks sufficient water. She has hypertension and takes amlodipine and atenolol. What is the most likely contributing factor?
explanation: Calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine commonly cause constipation (beta blockers can contribute); review the drug history first.
key_note: Age in the source was garbled ('10 year old woman'); stem rewritten.

stem: A 33 year old man, smoker, presented with 1 week history of persistent vomiting, anorexia, malaise and yellowness of the eyes. Likely diagnosis is
explanation: Anorexia, vomiting, malaise and jaundice over a week in a young adult is acute viral hepatitis.

stem: A 30-year-patient presents with 07 days history of yellow discoloration of eyes, anorexia, nausea and easy bruisability. He is suspected to have acute viral hepatitis. Likely cause may be?
explanation: Acute viral hepatitis with jaundice and anorexia in a young adult is most commonly hepatitis A; Wilson's disease is not a typical cause of acute hepatitis in this setting.

stem: In the causes of Acute Hepatitis, pick up the commonest cause:
explanation: Viral infection is the commonest cause of acute hepatitis worldwide and in Pakistan (A, B, E and C).

stem: Which statement does NOT favor Acute Hepatitis?

options.B: Prodromal features have lot of nausea and vomiting.
options.C: Fever seen in the prodromal phase.
options.E: Markedly raised S ALT and AST.

explanation: Recurrent biliary colic points to gallstone disease and obstructive jaundice, not acute hepatitis.

stem: Which of the following Liver function tests will be seen in "Acute Hepatitis"?

options.C: Hyperbilirubinemia with normal Serum ALT & raised ALP.

explanation: Acute hepatitis causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with markedly raised ALT/AST (hepatocellular picture).

stem: Pick up the statement indicating bad prognosis in Acute Hepatitis.

options.A: Severe vomiting leading to dehydration in prodromal phase.
options.C: Disturbed mental state a week after the onset of jaundice.
options.D: Pruritis occurring during the course of jaundice.
options.E: Hepatitis E in a non-pregnant female.

explanation: Encephalopathy (altered mental state) after the onset of jaundice indicates acute liver failure and a bad prognosis.

stem: A 20-year-male presents with yellow discoloration of sclera for 5 days. He denies any past significant history. Which of the following is a cause of acute hepatitis?
explanation: Cytomegalovirus is an infective cause of acute hepatitis; Wilson's disease, haemochromatosis and glycogen storage disease are metabolic, and autoimmune hepatitis is usually chronic.

stem: Which of the following is a cause of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia?
explanation: Viral hepatitis causes conjugated (hepatocellular and cholestatic) hyperbilirubinaemia; Gilbert's syndrome and neonatal jaundice are unconjugated.

stem: A 15-year boy presented in OPD with nausea and anorexia for 3 days and fever for 2 days. On examination he is jaundiced. Hepatitis A serology for IgM is positive. What complication can he develop with this condition?
explanation: Hepatitis A rarely causes fulminant hepatic failure (about 0.1-0.5%), and never chronic liver disease or carcinoma.

stem: A 24-year-old at 32 weeks' gestation presents with a week of fever, malaise, and jaundice. ALT 1,500 IU/L; INR 2.0; no encephalopathy at presentation. She drank untreated water during floods. HBsAg negative; anti-HEV IgM positive. What is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Acute hepatitis E infection in pregnancy

explanation: Hepatitis E (faeco-oral, flood water) is severe in pregnancy with a high risk of fulminant failure; IgM anti-HEV confirms it.

stem: A patient presents with jaundice: which of the following hepatitis frequently leads to fulminant hepatic failure;
explanation: Hepatitis B, especially with delta co-infection, is the commonest viral cause of fulminant hepatic failure among the options; hepatitis C very rarely causes it.

stem: A 26-year-old for premarital screening: HBsAg positive, anti-HBc IgM positive, anti-HBs negative, ALT mildly elevated. What does this serology most likely indicate?
explanation: HBsAg with IgM anti-HBc and no anti-HBs indicates acute hepatitis B; in chronic infection IgM anti-HBc is negative.

stem: A nurse with HBsAg positive, HBcAb IgG positive and HBeAg negative. What is most likely diagnosis?
explanation: HBsAg positive with anti-HBc IgG and HBeAg negative indicates the inactive carrier state (low replication); IgM anti-HBc would be expected in acute infection.

stem: A 40-year-patient scheduled for molar extraction. Which screening test you will order to rule out Hepatitis B
explanation: HBsAg is the screening test for hepatitis B infection.

stem: A 45-year-male presents with jaundice. His liver is found to be 5 cm with an enlarged spleen. and is diagnosed to have chronic hepatitis. Following can lead to Chronic Hepatitis in majority of cases'

options.E: Hepatitis E in a pregnant female.

explanation: Hepatitis C becomes chronic in about 75-85% of cases, far more than hepatitis B in adults (5-10%); hepatitis A and E never cause chronic hepatitis.
key_note: Paper key marked B (Hepatitis B); correct is D: hepatitis C leads to chronic hepatitis in the majority of cases.

stem: 50 years old female presented in OPD with low grade fever and generalized body aches. On investigation, anti-HCV AB was positive. What will be the most diagnostic test?
explanation: A positive anti-HCV only shows exposure; HCV RNA by PCR confirms active infection and guides treatment.

stem: A woman presented in OPD with abdominal distension for 2 months. On examination she had palmar erythema, spider naevi, moderate ascites and splenomegaly. Ultrasound showed a coarse liver and dilated portal vein. The most common cause of cirrhosis in Pakistan is:
explanation: Hepatitis C is the commonest cause of cirrhosis in Pakistan, followed by hepatitis B.

stem: A 50-year woman is found to have elevated aminotransferases and a fatty liver on imaging.She is obese and has type 2 diabetes mellitus. What is the most appropriate initial approach?
explanation: Lifestyle modification (weight loss, exercise, diet) is the first-line treatment of NAFLD/NASH; there is no role for antivirals.

stem: A 52-year-old woman is diagnosed with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis following a liver biopsy. What is the single most important step to help prevent the progression of her disease?
explanation: Weight loss (7-10% of body weight) with diet and exercise is the key measure to halt progression of NASH.

stem: A young patient presents as a follow-up case of fatty liver. He reports that he feels dragging sensation in right hypochondrium. Initially, the liver span can be measured in usual practice by;

options.C: X ray abdomen arrect and supine

explanation: Liver span is measured in routine practice by clinical examination (percussion and palpation); imaging is used only when needed.

stem: A 56-year-old lady presents to you with the history of progressive abdominal distention, oedema feet, generalized weakness and multiple episodes of hematemesis. Her examination showed ascites and splenomegaly, her JVP was not raised. Ascitic fluid R/E showed transudative ascites, what is the most likely cause of her presentation?
explanation: Transudative ascites with splenomegaly, haematemesis (varices) and a normal JVP indicates portal hypertension from cirrhosis; cardiac causes would show a raised JVP.

stem: Portal Hypertension is caused by all of the following except
explanation: Amoebic liver abscess does not cause portal hypertension; cirrhosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome and portal vein thrombosis do.

stem: A 55 year old man from hyderabad with a known history of hepatitis c presents with progressive abdominal distension and discomfort. He reports early satiety and difficulty breathing while lying flat. on examination he has shifting dullness, pedal edema, mild jaundice. Ultrasound confirms presence of Ascites & nodular liver. SAAG ratio is calculated To be >1.1g/dl, what is most likely underlying cause?
explanation: SAAG >1.1 g/dl indicates portal hypertension; with hepatitis C and a nodular liver the cause is cirrhosis.

stem: A patient with liver cirrhosis and ascites as admitted in your ward. Which of the following statements is correct regarding the diagnostic ascitic tap?

options.A: It is performed under general anaesthesia
options.B: Approx. 3 litres of ascitic fluid is aspirated
options.C: Can be performed safely in a patient with platelets < 10,000
options.E: Can be used to calculate SAAG ratio

explanation: Diagnostic paracentesis is done under local anaesthesia with a small sample and is used to calculate SAAG, cell count and culture.

stem: A 45-year male, known case of chronic liver disease secondary to HCV, presents with worsening ascites, fever, and abdominal pain. US: coarse shrunken liver, splenomegaly, gross free fluid. Labs: Hb 10.5, WCC 16000, platelets 122000, PT 18 sec, INR 1.4. Next investigation to establish diagnosis?
explanation: Fever, abdominal pain and ascites in a cirrhotic suggest SBP; diagnostic paracentesis with fluid cell count and culture is the next investigation.

stem: A 45-year-patient with liver disease presents with history of abdominal distension, pain abdomen and fever. There is no history of constipation. On examination you notice shifting dullness and mild tenderness in abdomen, liver is 5 cm in size, spleen is enlarged and bowel sounds are positive. Likely cause is;
explanation: Fever, abdominal pain and tender ascites in a patient with chronic liver disease is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis until proven otherwise.

stem: A 60-year-old woman diagnosed case of DCLD secondary to HCV presented in E.R with complaint of worsening of abdominal distension, abdominal pain and fever from last 3 days. Abdominal examination revealed generalized tenderness and distended abdomen with positive shifting dullness. Ascitic fluid analysis reveals a diagnosis of Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis. Which of the following organism is the most likely cause?
explanation: E. coli is the commonest cause of SBP, followed by Klebsiella and Streptococcus pneumoniae.
key_note: Age in the source was garbled ('6 year old'); stem corrected to 60 years.

stem: A 40-year-male is diagnosed with chronic Hepatitis C with liver cirrhosis. Which complication of hepatic cirrhosis is investigated by measuring alpha fetoprotein levels?
explanation: Alpha-fetoprotein with ultrasound is used for hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance in cirrhosis.

stem: A 70-year man presents in OPD with jaundice, dark urine, and abdominal distention for last 20 days. His medical history includes non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and recent weight loss.Laboratory tests indicate a high serum alpha-fetoprotein level. What is the most concerning possibility in this patient?
explanation: Raised AFP with jaundice, weight loss and background chronic liver disease points to hepatocellular carcinoma.

stem: A 56-years-man with Wilson disease presented with right upper quadrant discomfort. A ultrasound scan is performed and this demonstrates a mass lesion in the right lobe of liver. What is the most appropriate method of establishing the underlying diagnosis?
explanation: A new liver mass in a patient with chronic liver disease is investigated with AFP (with imaging); biopsy is reserved for doubtful cases because of bleeding and seeding risk.

stem: A patient came to you with resected colonic carcinoma. How do you follow up this patient for liver metastases
explanation: Ultrasound abdomen (or CT) is the routine non-invasive follow-up for liver metastases after colorectal resection; biopsy is not used for surveillance.
key_note: Paper keys marked C (Liver biopsy); correct is B: ultrasound is the follow-up imaging, biopsy is invasive and only for diagnosis.

stem: Which of the following medications reduced mortality in patients with portal hypertension in long term.
explanation: Long-term non-selective beta blockers (propranolol, carvedilol) reduce variceal bleeding and mortality in portal hypertension.

stem: A 54 year old man diagnosed case of decompensated chronic liver disease secondary to HBV infection presented with hematemesis associated with dizziness and syncope. He was resuscitated in the emergency with 2 L of saline, one unit of whole blood, high dose PPIs and terlipressin. He was not hemodynamically stable with B.P of 80/50 and Pulse rate of 115/min despite resuscitation. He was having persistent episodes of hematemesis. What is the next appropriate management step?

options.B: Pass Nasogastric tube and Gastric lavage
options.C: Pass Sengstaken Blakemore tube and Balloon tamponade
options.D: Urgent surgical consultation for exploratory laparotomy
options.E: Continue with the fluid and blood replacement

explanation: Persistent variceal bleeding with shock despite resuscitation, terlipressin and PPI needs a Sengstaken-Blakemore balloon tamponade as a bridge to endoscopic therapy or TIPS.

stem: A 50-year-old man with hepatitis C related cirrhosis presents with drowsiness for 3 days. He is vitally stable, drowsy but arousable, with spider angiomas, asterixis and ascites with shifting dullness. Labs: blood sugar 84 mg/dl, bilirubin 4.4 mg/dl, ALT 78 IU/L, Na 146 mEq/L, K 2.8 mEq/L. What is the next management step?
explanation: Hypokalaemia (K 2.8) precipitates and worsens hepatic encephalopathy by increasing renal ammonia production; correct it with IV potassium.

stem: 58 year old man with known hepatitis c related cirrhosis brought to ER by his family due to confusion, disorientation& flapping tremors. He was recently advised by a local practitioner to Increase protein Intake to build strength, His Ammonia level, are elevated. & he has no signs of infection/ GI bleeding. what is most likely precipitating factor for altered mental status?
explanation: Excess dietary protein increases the ammonia load and can precipitate encephalopathy; the stem excludes infection and bleeding.

stem: 60 years old male, diagnosed case of DCLD secondary to HCV, presented with anorexia and altered sensorium. Most likely precipitating factor in this patient is
explanation: Constipation increases ammonia absorption and is a common precipitant of hepatic encephalopathy; reduced sodium intake and more water are not precipitants.

stem: Which is a risk factor for gallstones?
explanation: Cystic fibrosis is a risk factor for gallstones (female sex, obesity, age, haemolysis and low-fibre diet are others).

stem: A patient presents with fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain after a recent travel history. Ultrasound shows gallstones and possible cholangitis. Which organism is most likely responsible?
explanation: E. coli is the commonest organism in cholangitis, followed by Klebsiella and Enterococcus.

stem: A 37-year-male presents with yellow discoloration of eyes and urine. Which combination of features specifically explain obstructive jaundice?
explanation: Pruritus and clay-coloured stools reflect bile salt retention and absent stercobilin, specific for obstructive jaundice.

stem: Which of the following diseases can present with obstructive jaundice?
explanation: Bile duct stenosis is a cause of obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice; carcinoma of the head, not the tail, of the pancreas obstructs the CBD.

stem: A 65-year woman presents in ER with jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, and pruritus for last 01 month. Imaging studies show strictures of the bile ducts and a "beading" appearance on cholangiography. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Beaded strictures of bile ducts on cholangiography indicate primary sclerosing cholangitis.

stem: A 35-year woman presents in OPD with elevated liver enzymes, facial redness, and spider angiomas. She has an enlarged liver and her family history reveals multiple relatives with liver problems. Tests reveal anti-smooth muscle antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A young woman with hepatitis, positive anti-smooth muscle antibody and family history suggests autoimmune hepatitis.

stem: A 42-year female presents with generalized pruritus, mild scleral icterus. Physical examination: hepatomegaly, palmar erythema, spider angiomas. Labs: total bilirubin 3.5 mg/dl, ALT 105 IU/L, AST 100 IU/L, ALP 382 IU/L, GGT 596 IU/L. Ultrasound: normal gall bladder and CBD. Next investigation?
explanation: With a cholestatic picture and a normal biliary tree on ultrasound, liver biopsy is the answer given in the paper key; AMA is the usual first test for PBC.
key_note: AMA is not among the options; paper key D (liver biopsy) kept.

stem: A 45 year old man comes to your office for a follow up visit. One year ago he was diagnosed with hereditary hemochromatosis. He has been treated by phlebotomy with one unit of blood removed every week for the past year. His most recent lab values are: Hemoglobin 12.0 g/dl; Hematocrit 36%; Serum Ferritin 50ng/ml; Serum Iron 100microgram/dl; Serum TIBC 260mg/dl. What is the most appropriate next step in therapy?

options.B: Liver biopsy to assess hepatic iron overload
options.D: Phlebotomy 1 unit every 2 weeks until the Hemoglobin is less than 10.0 g/dl
options.E: Phlebotomy 1 unit every 2 weeks until the serum iron level is less than 20 microgram/ dl

explanation: Once ferritin is at target (50-100 ng/ml), maintenance phlebotomy is about 1 unit every 3 months to keep ferritin low.

stem: A 43-year-old female was screened for haemochromatosis on a background of positive family history. She was found to have raised iron stores and further testing. She was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus recently and dilated cardiomyopathy. She was reviewed by the hepatology team who arranged for venesection to be carried out as part of the management plan. What would the most appropriate marker to monitor response to treatment?
explanation: Serum ferritin (with transferrin saturation) is the marker used to monitor venesection in haemochromatosis.

stem: Which one of the following metabolic disorders is least likely to cause malabsorption?
explanation: Haemochromatosis does not cause malabsorption; cystic fibrosis, PBC (bile salt deficiency), lactose intolerance and Whipple's disease do.

stem: Which one of the following is most suggestive of Wilson's disease?
explanation: Low serum caeruloplasmin is the most suggestive finding in Wilson's disease; hepatic copper and urinary copper are raised.

stem: Wilsons disease is a metabolic disorder characterized by neurological and hepatic clinical features. It is caused by abnormal accumulation of;
explanation: Wilson's disease is caused by copper accumulation (ATP7B defect), affecting liver, brain and cornea.

stem: A 60-year-old female presents with abdominal pain and gradually increasing ascites with diffuse abdominal tenderness. Ascitic fluid shows an exudate with predominant lymphocytes and atypical cells. The most likely diagnosis is:
explanation: Atypical (malignant) cells in a lymphocytic exudate indicate malignant ascites; TB ascites shows lymphocytes without atypical cells and SBP is neutrophilic.
